name: numeric-sort-comparator
diff:
diff --git a/src/scores.js b/src/scores.js
--- a/src/scores.js
+++ b/src/scores.js
@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
 export function topScores(scores, n) {
-  return scores.sort().reverse().slice(0, n)
+  return [...scores].sort((a, b) => b - a).slice(0, n)
 }

question.prompt: topScores([9, 10, 100, 2], 2): what did the old code return, what does the new code return, and what else does the new version stop doing to the caller's array?
question.answerKey: The old code sorted the numbers as strings, so [9, 10, 100, 2] became [10, 100, 2, 9], reversed to [9, 2, 100, 10], and it returned [9, 2]. The new code sorts numerically, largest first, and returns [100, 10]. It also sorts a copy, so the caller's array is no longer reordered.
rubric: the old default sort compared the numbers as strings and returned the wrong top scores, [9, 2]
the comparator sorts numerically and returns [100, 10]
spreading into a new array stops sort from reordering the caller's array

answers.text: Old: sort() compares as strings so you get [9, 2]. New: numeric descending gives [100, 10], and [...scores] means the input array is not reordered any more.
before [9,2] (lexicographic sort), after [100,10]; also no in-place mutation of scores thanks to the copy
Both return [100, 10]; the change only avoids changing the input array.
The old code returned [9, 2] because of string sorting, and the new code returns [100, 10].
